claims.claim: On the eve of European contact the Americas held roughly 60 million people (about 60.5 million, IQR 44.8-78.2 million), comparable to Europe at the time, refuting the idea of a sparsely populated wilderness.

North America before contact contained hundreds of distinct nations and languages organized in many political forms, from small autonomous clans to cities and confederacies; among Eastern Woodland peoples such as the Iroquois, Lenape, Muscogee, and Cherokee, women often held real political power.

The Ancestral Puebloans of the Southwest built cliff and multi-story dwellings and roads running some 180 miles; Chaco Canyon became their administrative, religious, and cultural center by about 1050 CE, and the towns were abandoned about a century later, probably because of drought.

Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was a Mississippian city with more than ten thousand residents at its peak around 1100 CE (tens of thousands more on surrounding farms) and roughly 120 earthen mounds; its central tract covers about 2,200 acres and it was larger than London was in AD 1250; the civilization declined after 1300 CE.

The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois/Six Nations) Confederacy united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca (later joined by the Tuscarora) under the Great Law of Peace, with fifty hereditary chiefs (9 Mohawk, 9 Oneida, 14 Onondaga, 10 Cayuga, 8 Seneca) chosen by clan mothers and meeting in a Grand Council; the confederacy continues today.

In 1988 the U.S. Congress passed H.Con.Res.331 (100th Congress) acknowledging the contribution of the Iroquois Confederacy to the development of the U.S. Constitution and reaffirming the government-to-government relationship between Indian tribes and the United States.

The 'Three Sisters' (corn, beans, and squash) were planted together: the corn provides a trellis for climbing beans, the beans fix nitrogen that enriches the soil, and the squash's broad leaves shade the ground to hold moisture and suppress weeds.

European contact introduced Old World diseases (smallpox, measles, mumps, chickenpox) to which Native peoples had no immunity; one peer-reviewed estimate is that the Indigenous population of the Americas fell by about 90 percent (IQR 87-92%), from roughly 60 million to about 6 million, within roughly a century, worsened by warfare, enslavement, famine, and displacement.

Native nations did not vanish; the United States federally recognizes more than 570 tribal nations that retain inherent powers of self-government and a government-to-government relationship with the federal government.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How directly the Haudenosaunee Confederacy influenced the U.S. Constitution
positions: Congress in 1988 (H.Con.Res.331) formally acknowledged a contribution to the development of the Constitution
Many historians consider a direct, documented causal influence weak or overstated, while acknowledging that framers such as Franklin knew of and admired the Confederacy
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that the resolution was passed and that historians debate how direct the influence was, without asserting a settled causal claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact count of federally recognized tribes
positions: The BIA FAQ page states 575 federally recognized tribes and villages
The most recent annual Federal Register list (2024) enumerates 574
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the conservative, durable phrasing 'more than 570' in learner-facing text; the small year-to-year variation is noted here.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Indigenous North America is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive, verifiable historical content; essentially all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic placeholder definitions with specific, sourced history of Indigenous North America.

Added the population scale, culture-region diversity, Cahokia, Ancestral Puebloans, Haudenosaunee governance, Three Sisters agriculture, the disease catastrophe, and the survival of sovereign nations, none of which appeared in the draft.

sourceRecords.title: Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492
sourceRecords.provider: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis, Quaternary Science Reviews 207:13-36 (peer-reviewed)
sourceRecords.notes: Findings verified via WebSearch summaries of the published paper and the UCL news release on 2026-08-20 (the ScienceDirect full text is paywalled). Supports: a pre-1492 population estimate of about 60.5 million (IQR 44.8-78.2 million) based on 119 regional estimates; and a decline of about 90 percent (IQR 87-92%) over the century after contact, from roughly 60 million to about 6 million by 1600, from epidemics compounded by warfare and famine. Figures cited and attributed; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Confederacy's Creation
sourceRecords.provider: Haudenosaunee Confederacy (official website of the Confederacy)
sourceRecords.notes: Read on 2026-08-20 via curl with a browser user-agent (WebFetch route). The Confederacy's own account. Supports: the Peacemaker, with Hiawatha (Aiionwatha), founded the Confederacy uniting the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca; the fifty hereditary chief titles distributed as 9 Mohawk, 9 Oneida, 14 Onondaga, 10 Cayuga, and 8 Seneca; chiefs chosen by clan mothers; and that the Confederacy 'thrives today' as the Six Nations' representative government. Centered as an Indigenous-voice source; no wording reproduced.
